Petrography and geochemistry Marathon dykes are quartz tholeiites that consist largely of equigranular to subophitic clinopyroxene and plagioclase in approximately equal proportions. Lesser amounts of amphi- Me, magnetite, myrmekite, quartz, biotite, and apatite, in approximate order of decreasing abundance, have an aggre- gate modal content of about 10 - 15 76. The plagioclase is variably altered to saussurite, and the clinopyroxene to turgid aggregates. The pyroxene is locally rimmed by a green amphibole, the development of which increases in proximity to myrmekite and quartz development. Zircon and bad- deleyite, with pleochroic haloes, occur in coarse-grained interiors at sites 4, 1 1, 17 - 24, 26, and 28, particularly in the amphibole, but also in biotite, indicating that many of the wider Marathon dykes have potential for U-Pb dating.

characteristics of the region and describe the paleomagnetism of the plutonic rocks there. Finally, we describe how structural analysis may be used to correct discordant paleomagnetic directions. Tectonic Setting and Major Structures The study area lies within the eastern part of the Inter- montane Belt in north-central British Columbia (Figure 1) and straddles the boundary between the Quesnellia and Stikinia tectonostratigraphic terranes [Monger, 1984]. Stikinia, Cache Creek, Quesnellia, and Slide Mountain terranes had been essentially amalgamated by the Early Jurassic due to the closing of the Cache Creek ocean, forming the composite Terrane I, and were subsequently accreted to the ancient margin of North America during Middle Jurassic contraction [Monger, 1984]. Transcurrent motions between the Inter- montane Belt and North American craton occurred in the Late Cretaceous to Eocene at a time when the Kula plate in the west was converging obliquely with the North American plate [Engebretson et al., 1985; Umhoefer, 1987]. These motions apparently have produced dextral strike-slip displacements along the Tintina trench and northern Rocky Mountain trench (TT-NRMT) fault zone [Roddick, 1967; Tempelman-Kluit, 1979; Gabrielse, 1985; Struik, 1993] and a sequence of fa

ip faults trending east-northeast (Figure 2), as well as some large-scale northwest to north-northwest trending folds. Based on their geometric and spatial relationships, all these faults can be related to the stress field associated with movement on the FIF [Zhang and Hynes, 1994]. Strain analysis of the deformed volcanic fragments along one of the north-northwest trending, dextral strike-slip faults shows that the principal orientations of the strain ellipsoids are in accordance with those of the magnetic susceptibility ellipsoids from the adjacent deformed dioritic rocks, indicating that the plutonic rocks experienced the same deformation as the Late Triassic Takla Group volcanics [Zhang and Hynes, 1994]. The dextral displacement of --110 km along the FIF probably took place during middle Cretaceous or Late Cretaceous time, based on its crosscutting relationship with the Kutcho and Pinchi faults [Gabrielse, 1985]. The strike- slip faulting in the study area may therefore not have been earlier than middle Cretaceous as Early Jurassic to Cretaceous dioritic rocks were involved in the faulting in many places. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Mesozoic rocks from the Sierra de Los Organos and Sierra del Rosario fold belts of western Cuba revealed postfolding magnetisation in diabases of the Late Jurassic E1 SAbalo Formation and carbonates of the middle Cretaceous Pons and the Late Cretaceous Carmita and Moreno formations. Steep components with inclinations of about 70 ° were isolated from all three formations; at the same time, postfolding shallow components were also found in a few samples of the Pons limestones. We rule out a possibility to account for these results by either horizontal movements or non-dipole field anomaly. Neither very appealing is a hypothesis of a post-remagnetization tilt of the entire region. All the components appear to be confined to a plane perpendicular to the main structural trends; we hypothesize that the remanences might have been distorted or re-aligned during deformation; this assumption, however, is far from being proven. In contrast, well-defined characteristic components were isolated from basaits of the Aptian-Albian Encrucijada (D/I = 2470/23 °, K= 14, a95 z 9.0 °) and the Late Cretaceous Orozco (D/l= 2280/22 °, K= 110, a95 = 4.7) formations from the Bahia Honda zone in the north of western Cuba; the remanence in the Encrucijada Formation is shown to predate deformation. Mean inclinations in both formations match those in Cretaceous volcanics from central Cuba, and all the results show lower latitudes than expected from the reference data

E1 SAbalo Formation and carbonates of the middle Cretaceous Pons and the Late Cretaceous Carmita and Moreno formations. Steep components with inclinations of about 70 ° were isolated from all three formations; at the same time, postfolding shallow components were also found in a few samples of the Pons limestones. We rule out a possibility to account for these results by either horizontal movements or non-dipole field anomaly. Neither very appealing is a hypothesis of a post-remagnetization tilt of the entire region. All the components appear to be confined to a plane perpendicular to the main structural trends; we hypothesize that the remanences might have been distorted or re-aligned during deformation; this assumption, however, is far from being proven. E1 SAbalo Formation and carbonates of the middle Cretaceous Pons and the Late Cretaceous Carmita and Moreno formations. Steep components with inclinations of about 70 ° were isolated from all three formations; at the same time, postfolding shallow components were also found in a few samples of the Pons limestones. We rule out a possibility to account for these results by either horizontal movements or non-dipole field anomaly. Neither very appealing is a hypothesis of a post-remagnetization tilt of the entire region. All the components appear to be confined to a plane perpendicular to the main structural trends; we hypothesize that the remanences might have been distorted or re-aligned during deformation; this assumption, however, is far from being proven. Mean inclinations in both formations match those in Cretaceous volcanics from central Cuba, and all the results show lower latitudes than expected from the reference data for the North American plate thus implying that volcanic domains of Cuba were displaced northward by about 1000 km prior to the Middle Eocene. Such a pattern, however, has never been observed either in the field or laboratory experiments (Klig- field et al., 1983; Cogne and Perroud, 1987). The strain hypothesis, however, infers strong internal de- formation, but neither cleavage nor other types of internal deformation were observed in either forma- tion. Besides, any internal deformation could hardly be so uniform as to result in close agreement of paleomagnetic directions from the sections about 100 km apart. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility might have been of help for testing the strain hypothesis; unfortunately, these sediments are very weakly mag- netized, and AMS measurements could not be per- formed. Nevertheless, the hypothesis that observed pattern of paleomagnetic directions is related to the deformational process cannot now be discarded. In principle, it is possible that the studied forma- tions were tilted after thrusting and folding and acquisition of remanence because the precise posi- tion of a rock mass with respect to the paleohorizon- tal is unknown for a postfolding component. Steep components with inclinations of about 70 ° were isolated from all three formations; at the same time, postfolding shallow components were also found in a few samples of the Pons limestones. November 1995 Abstract Palaeomagnetic studies have been carried out on mid-Cretaceous to latest Palaeocene sediments from the Tethyan Himalaya on the northern margin of the Indian Plate near the localities of Gamba (28.3°N, 88.5°E) and Duela (28.0°N, 89.2°E) in southern Tibet. A total of 61 sites (more than 700 cores) have been sampled mainly from limestones (Zongshan Formation, Jidula Formation Member II, Zongpu Formation), sandstones (Jidula Formation Member III) and graywackes (Gamba Group Member II), with ages well defined from detailed lithological and biostratigraphic analyses. Carriers of characteristic remanences are magnetite in limestones and graywackes, and hematite in sandstones. Reliable palaeodirections were obtained from 35 sites (356 specimens). Positive fold tests, antiparallel normal and reverse polarities, a northward trend of the palaeolatitudes with decreasing age, and absence of any metamorphic overprint indicate a primary origin for the characteristic remanences. The results have been compared with expected palaeodirections according to available data for the Indian subcontinent based on its present-day geometry. After removal of goethite remanences through heating above 100°C, remanence directions remained stable up to about 650°C (Fig. 9a and b). ChRM directions, carried by hematite (and probably also by magnetite in some of the specimens) were determined from demagnetization data obtained after the 200°C heating step. In the limestones magnetite is dominant with a minor hematite component, identified by low coer- civity combined with unblocking temperatures < around 500°C and high coercivity combined with unblocking temperatures > 600°C, respectively (Fig. 4c, specimen B8). AF demagnetization usually re- vealed two components (Fig. 9d-f). After removal of a soft component with scattered directions a harder component is demagnetized between 20 and 100 mT. Carriers of characteristic remanences are magnetite in limestones and graywackes, and hematite in sandstones. Reliable palaeodirections were obtained from 35 sites (356 specimens). Positive fold tests, antiparallel normal and reverse polarities, a northward trend of the palaeolatitudes with decreasing age, and absence of any metamorphic overprint indicate a primary origin for the characteristic remanences. The results have been compared with expected palaeodirections according to available data for the Indian subcontinent based on its present-day geometry. The late Maastrichtian sites (fourteen sites, 156 specimens) and the middle-Late Palaeocene sites (fourteen sites, 113 specimens) yield palaeolatitudes of 5.7°S and 4.0°N for the sampling localities in southern Tibet, respectively. These palaeolatitudes are much further north than expected and imply that crustal shortening between the Tethyan Himalaya and the Indian Shield since the time of India-Eurasia collision has occurred on the order of 1500 km at the longitude of Gamba/Duela.

carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: significant drop in the drift rate from nearly 20 to less than 5 cm/yr at 55-50 Ma is mostly interpreted as the onset of the collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate (e.g., Patriat and Achache, 1984; Besse and Courtillot, 1988). The initial collision occurred in the western part with progressive closure of the Neo-Tethyan ocean from west to east (Klootwijk et al., 1985). Further conver- gence led to straightforward and rotational under- thrusting of the Indian Plate beneath the southern Eurasian margin since the Miocene. During the past years an earlier age for the collision has been pro- posed. Based on a review of primary and secondary palaeoremanences from the Himalaya and Hin- dukush and results from the Ninetyeast Ridge, Klootwijk et al. (1991, 1992) concluded that initial contact between India and Eurasia was already estab- lished at the Cretaceous/Tertiary time boundary. They interpret the drop in drift rate at 55-50 Ma as completion of closure of the Neo-Tethys. Occurrence of high-pressure rocks of eclogite facies in the Upper Kaghan Valley (northwestern Himalaya) with a peak metamorphic age of 49_ 6 Ma (Tonarini et al., 1993; Spencer, 1993) supports the hypothesis of an initial collision as early as 65 Ma in the western part. from limestones (Zongshan Formation, Jidula Formation Member II, Zongpu Formation), sandstones (Jidula Formation Member III) and graywackes (Gamba Group Member II), with ages well defined from detailed lithological and biostratigraphic analyses. Carriers of characteristic remanences are magnetite in limestones and graywackes, and hematite in sandstones. Reliable palaeodirections were obtained from 35 sites (356 specimens). Positive fold tests, antiparallel normal and reverse polarities, a northward trend of the palaeolatitudes with decreasing age, and absence of any metamorphic overprint indicate a primary origin for the characteristic remanences. The results have been compared with expected palaeodirections according to available data for the Indian subcontinent based on its present-day geometry. The late Maastrichtian sites (fourteen sites, 156 specimens) and the middle-Late Palaeocene sites (fourteen sites, 113 specimens) yield palaeolatitudes of 5.7°S and 4.0°N for the sampling localities in southern Tibet, respectively. These palaeolatitudes are much further north than expected and imply that crustal shortening between the Tethyan Himalaya and the Indian Shield since the time of India-Eurasia collision has occurred on the order of 1500 km at the longitude of Gamba/Duela.

The occurrence of cooke'ite allows us to estimate the maximum temperature for the metamor- phism at around 325°C. The pressure estimated from fluid inclusion studies (Bernard, 1978; Jenatton, 1981; Nziengui, 1993) is around 200 MPa. This metamorphism is dated at around 26.5 Ma by Nzien- gui (1993). Thus the NRM carried by extremely stable fine-grained, probably single domain, pyrrhotite (Rochette and Lamarche, 1986 and Ro- chette et al., 1990) with a Curie temperature between 310°C and 335°C (Fig. 2a), is probably a thermore- manent magnetization (TRM) acquired during post metamorphic cooling. The occurence of antipodal normal and reverse polarities as a function of the altitude especialy in area 1 and 2 (Table 1), supports this interpretation. Moreover, the study of Rochette et al. (1992) in the same black schist facies but in the northern valley of Maurienne has shown the record of successive normal and reverse components versus temperature in the same sample, therefore strongly supporting our contention that NRM is a TRM. Even if a metamorphic CRM (chemical remanent magneti- za

ion) was responsible for our NRM, the directional interpretation would be identical. 3. Sampling and measurement We sampled 310 oriented cores in 44 sites from the Bourg d'Oisans area (Fig. 1), where the Liassic marly limestone facies is very well exposed. For each site we cored between 5 and 14 samples with a portable drill and oriented them with a magnetic compass. Local structural measurements were taken, in order to make corrections for bedding (SO) and cleavage (S 1). NRM measurements were carried out with a Mol- spin spinner magnetometer initially and after treat- ment at 150°C. For 1 or 2 specimens per site a progressive thermal demagnetization up to 350°C was carried out with the use of a CTF cryogenic magnetometer. The furnace used was a Pyrox fabri- cation and allowed us to heat 30 to 40 specimens in the same time. The residual field inside was less than about 10 nT. The susceptibility was measured using MS2 Bartington, after each heating step. Results from 5 sites with very low intensity of magnetization (< 0.05 mA/m), have not been taken into account in this study. Site mean directions for the characteris- tic remanent magnetization (ChRM) were deter- mined through Fisher (1953) statistics on the direc- tion remaining after demagnetization at 150°C (Table 1). Crouzet a,*, G. Mrnard a,1, p. Rochette b,2 a Laboratoire de G£odynamique de Cha'ines Alpines, UPRES-A 5025 du CNRS, UniversiM de Savoie, 73376 Le Bourget du Lac, France b CEREGE, URA 132 du CNRS, Universit£ Aix-Marseille 111, Plateau d'Arbois, BP 80, 13545 Aix en Provence, France Received 12 October 1995 Abstract In order to test the occurrence of post metamorphic rotations or tiltings, a paleomagnetic study was undertaken in 44 sites from the inverted half graben of Bourg d'Oisans ("Zone Dauphinoise", Western Alps). The magnetization carried by pyrrhotite was acquired after metamorphic culmination, around the Oligo-Miocene limit. No obvious rotations around a vertical axis, are recorded. Instead, the dispersion of paleomagnetic data is interpreted as due to a variable tilting around a horizontal N20E axis, consistent with structural observations. This gentle folding in the sedimentary cover is probably associated with thrusting of the Belledonne external crystalline massif over the foreland basement. The age of the tiltings reported in this paper is estimated as b

etamorphic age, can be used as a tectonic marker of the late history of a collision belt. In the Western Alps, the discovery of such a paleomagnetic signal carried by pyrrhotite (Rochette and Lamarche, 1986; Lamarche et al., 1988) allows us to test the existence of rotations around vertical or horizontal axes which occured after the cooling of these rocks. Pyrrhotite derives from the transformation of sedi- mentary magnetite during alpine metamorphism. * Corresponding author. Tel: (33)/79-75-88-77. Fax: (33)/79- 75-87-77. A detailed stratigraphic and bio- stratigraphic description of these exposures has been made by Mjagkova et al. (1963, 1977; in Russian) and Kanygin, Moscalenko & Yadrenkina (1987; in English). The Moyero region, as all of the Siberian platform, was an epicontinental sedimentation zone during the early Palaeozoic. The biostratigraphic data, based on conodonts and some macrofossils (e.g. brachiopods and cephalopods), indicate that 12 Ordovician stratigraphic horizons are present in the Moyero composite section, making it one of the best Ordovician sections from Eurasia in terms of dating and stratigraphic completeness (Kanygin et u1. 1987). However, a large strati- graphic gap is observed at the Ordovician/Silurian boundary. This hiatus is linked to the major oceanic regression that occurred during the uppermost Ordovician. In Moyero, this regression is marked by altered rocks indicating an emersion (and erosion) of long duration. The biostratigraphic data show that a record of the second half of the upper Ordovician and the lowermost Silurian is missing. Other sedimentary gaps probably exist within the Ordovician series, for example at the Llanvirn/Llandeilo boundary, but they seem to be of limited duration (Mjagkova et al. 1963, 1977). The Moyero river is located near the Siberian traps, which were dated recently at around 250Ma, close to the Permo- Triassic boundary (Claoue-Long et al. 1991; Renne & Basu 1991). Traces of these traps are observed in some exposures of the Moyero section, in the form of sills or dykes, which vary in thickness and lateral extent from decimetres to kilometres. In particular, the outcrops of Tremadoc age (lower Ordovician) are widely intruded by the traps. The sampled strata dip gently, on the order of 2-3", to the south-west. The northward flowing Moyero river cuts these strata and exposes successively Silurian to Cambrian levels (Fig. 1). Small oriented blocks were collected from 12 sections among the sites already listed and numbered by Mjagkova et ul. (1963, 1977; Fig. 2).
